• Foster data-driven adaptive change management within the overall health system | PATH Defining and building a data use culture; MEASURE data demand and use of resources; WHO SCORE; WHO M&E digital health interventions | | **PHASE 07: IMPLEMENTING, MAINTAINING AND SCALING** | • Maintain and sustain digital health implementations
• Identify risks and appropriate mitigations | Digital implementation investment guide; Asian Development Bank total cost of ownership tool; WHO handbook for health supply chain architecture; WHO handbook for health product catalogue (this document); WHO MAPS toolkit; WHO handbook for digitalizing primary health care; Be He@lthy, Be Mobile handbooks; Digital Square global goods guidebook; Principles for donor alignment | *Source: adapted from the 2020 WHO Digital Implementation Investment Guide (1).* ## SMART Guidelines This handbook is developed to complement the WHO’s Standards-based, Machine-readable, Adaptive, Requirements-based, and Testable (SMART) Guidelines initiative by providing guidance on NPC implementations that align with digital health implementations.
SMART Guidelines are a structured approach to integrating recommended public health and clinical practices into digital systems.
They represent the WHO’s approach to systematising and accelerating the consistent application of recommended, life-saving interventions in the digital age.
The five knowledge layers include: 1. **L1 – Narrative:** enhanced clinical, public health guidelines and structured data recommendations.

These layers guide stakeholders on translating recommendations into specifications and standards, technical specialists on integrating recommendations into updatable digital systems, and countries on localising, institutionalising, and updating digital systems while maintaining consistency with evidence-based recommendations (Figure 5).15 Fig.

5: WHO SMART Guidelines Approach | Layer | Knowledge layers and associated products (RESEARCH AND EVIDENCE BASE) | Country implementation (LOCALISATION) | | --- | --- | --- | | **L1: Narrative** | Guideline and data recommendations: Enhanced guidelines | **L1: Adaptation** — National policies, guidelines, data, and operational procedures | | **L2: Operational** | Semi-structured documentation of operational and functional requirements: Digital adaptation kits | **L2: Adaptation** — Localised requirements | | **L3: Machine readable** | Structured, software-neutral, specifications, code, terminology and interoperability standards: Machine-readable recommendations | **L3: Adaptation** — Localised machine readable code and standards | | **L4: Executable** | Software that is able to execute static algorithms and interoperable digital components and deliver operational and functional requirements: Reference software | **L4: Adaptation** — Localised static digital services and applications within a digital health enterprise | | **L5: Dynamic** | Executable dynamic algorithms that are trained and optimised with advanced analytics to achieve prioritised outcomes: Precision health models | **L5: Adaptation** — Dynamic digital applications and services trained and optimised for prioritised local outcomes | The focus of SMART Guidelines is on digital capabilities for healthcare.
Specifically, they define recommended public health and clinical business processes using structured, task-based workflows.

• Terms of reference (TOR) for master data governance group | ### Key elements of master data management procedures *Master data management procedures should include the following key elements to continuously and securely maintain master data: - **Data governance framework:** Establish clear policies, roles, responsibilities, and processes to ensure data quality and consistency for use across the health supply chain. - **Illustrative data management roles:** - **Data owner:** responsible for the overall strategy, governance, and quality of the product master data.
sentences.sectionTitle: Step 1. Define product master data management procedures

sentences.text: The data owner: - Defines the rules, policies, and standards for data quality, structure, and governance. - Makes decisions on how the data should be managed and ensures alignment with business objectives. - Approves changes to the product master data and ensures compliance with regulatory and business requirements. - Is accountable for the accuracy, completeness, and relevance of the product data in the organization. - **Data custodian:** responsible for the technical management and security of product master data.
sentences.sectionTitle: Step 1. Define product master data management procedures

- Data harmonization activities must consider all sources of product data, as well as the systems, processes, and organizations or stakeholders that will utilize this data.

sentences.text: This combination of attributes and codes facilitates comprehensive identification of products. - Generic national product codes, including drug codes and medicinal product identifiers (when using the WHO Drug Dictionary), should be mapped to trade item-specific identifiers, such as GTINs, or similar unique identifiers where GTINs are not available. - The product coding system should maintain uniform code lengths and ensure scalability to accommodate an increasing number of unique products. - Product master data structures should support the mapping of one generic national product code to multiple corresponding trade items.
